cards.headline: When you greet a group
cards.note: For two or more people, you say «están» and «les». Mexicans do this even with friends and children.

cards.headline: Hello at any hour
cards.note: Días lasts until about noon, tardes runs from noon to dark, and noches starts once it's dark. Noches also works as a goodbye. Buenas alone fits any hour.

cards.headline: Formal and informal
cards.note: Use usted with shopkeepers, older people and strangers; tú with friends and children. In Mexico, usted is a sign of respect, not distance.

rows.en: Good morning, ma'am. How are you?

rows.text: Hasta luego. Que le vaya bien.

cards.headline: When someone asks how you are
cards.note: To say how you are, you use «estoy».

cards.headline: Asking how someone is
cards.note: The question changes between está and estás, but your own answer always uses «estoy».

cards.headline: A small word
cards.note: ¿Mande? answers when someone calls you, and it also asks for a repeat. With older people, ¿mande? or ¿perdón? sounds polite.

rows.en: What do you want in your tacos?
Could you say that again, please?
Could you write it for me?

cards.headline: Formal and informal

rows.en: Can you say it again? · formal
Can you say it again? · informal

cards.note: With a neighbour or a friend, use puedes instead of puede. Me lo stays together, right before the verb.

cards.headline: When you leave a shop

rows.text: Hasta luego. Que le vaya bien.

cards.note: Igualmente means "same to you." When someone wishes you well with this phrase, answer "Gracias, igualmente."

cards.headline: Say it to one person or many

rows.en: Have a good day. · a friend
Have a good day. · a group

cards.note: Learn it as one whole phrase. Only the small word changes: le, te or les.

cards.headline: When you need a hand
cards.note: After puede, the next verb stays in its -r form: ayudar, hablar, repetir.

cards.headline: Formal and informal
cards.note: Use puede for someone you address as usted, and puedes for a neighbour.

cards.headline: Formal and informal
cards.note: Use usted with an older lady or someone you don't know, and tú with someone your own age.

cards.headline: When you meet someone

rows.en: My name's Rosa. Nice to meet you.

cards.note: Names go with me llamo, and the me is always there.

cards.headline: When you say where you're from

rows.text: Soy de Canadá, pero ahora vivo aquí.
rows.en: I'm from Canada, but I live here now.

cards.note: Soy de plus a city or a country tells where you come from.

cards.headline: Formal and informal
cards.note: Same question, two ways. Either way, you answer with Soy de plus a place.

cards.headline: When you spell your name

rows.en: Could you spell your surname, please?

rows.text: Doble u, e, be grande, be grande.

cards.note: Spanish letters have their own names. W is doble u, and the vowels sound like eh and ee, so spelling aloud sounds different from English.

cards.headline: Telling B from V

rows.text: ¿Con be grande o con ve chica?
rows.en: With big B or little V?

cards.note: B and V sound the same in Spanish, so Mexicans say be grande and ve chica to tell them apart.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every address includes the colonia, the neighbourhood. It matters more than the street name for finding a place, so people often answer with the colonia first.

cards.headline: When you meet someone new

rows.en: How long have you been here?

cards.note: The question word comes first and carries a written accent: cómo, dónde, cuánto. For origin, de goes in front: ¿de dónde eres?

cards.headline: When someone asks how long you've been here

rows.en: How long have you been in Mexico?
I've been in Mexico a month.

cards.note: Say llevo or tengo plus the time, then aquí or en México. Llevo dos semanas aquí works just as well.

cards.headline: Formal and informal

rows.en: How long have you been in Mexico? · formal
How long have you been in Mexico? · informal

cards.note: Lleva is for someone you address as usted, llevas for someone you address as tú.

cards.headline: Excuse me, or sorry?

rows.en: Excuse me: getting past or leaving.
Sorry: after a bump or a mistake.

cards.note: Mexican courtesy is constant and small. People say con permiso whenever they pass someone or leave a table.

cards.headline: Excuse me: who you're calling

rows.en: Excuse me, can you help me? · informal

cards.note: Use disculpe with a shopkeeper or stranger. Use disculpa with friends and people your age who say tú. Use disculpen when you call out to a group.

cards.headline: A small ending

rows.en: Right now. / In a little while.

cards.note: Adding -ito makes a request or an amount sound smaller and politer. It isn't literal: un momentito can be several minutes, and ahorita can mean now, soon or later.

cards.headline: Calling people by title

rows.en: Excuse me, young man, could you help me?

cards.note: Use joven, señor or señora for people you don't know. Use don or doña with the first name for older people you know.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Market staff often call you joven, señorita, güero or güera as they call you over. It's friendly sales talk.

cards.headline: When a shop asks what you need

rows.en: Come in! What were you looking for?

cards.note: Shop and market staff call out ¡pásele! to bring you in.

cards.headline: Two ways to answer a shop
cards.note: Shop staff ask in the past to sound softer. You just answer in the present: say what you want, or say you're just looking.

cards.headline: Saying one of something

rows.text: Me da un limón, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have one lime, please?

rows.text: Me da una torta de milanesa.
rows.en: Can I have a milanesa torta?

rows.text: Un agua de horchata, por favor.

cards.note: Use un for one, and una for a feminine word like torta. Agua is the exception: the phrase is un agua.

cards.headline: Saying more than one

rows.en: How many tacos do you want?

rows.text: Me da dos tacos, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have two tacos, please?

rows.text: Me da dos limones, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have two limes, please?

cards.note: To make more than one, add -s after a vowel, as in tacos, and -es after a consonant, as in limones.

cards.headline: Name the filling

rows.text: Me da tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have three al pastor tacos, please?

rows.text: Una torta de jamón, por favor.
Un agua de jamaica, por favor.

cards.note: The food comes first, then de, then the filling or flavour. Spanish puts the filling after the food, the other way round from English.

rows.en: Hi! What can I get you?

rows.text: Me da tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have three al pastor tacos, please?

cards.headline: Ordering politely with

rows.text: Me da un café, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have a coffee, please?

rows.text: Me da una torta para llevar.
rows.en: Can I have a torta to go?

rows.text: Me da tres tacos de pastor, por favor.
rows.en: Can I have three al pastor tacos, please?

cards.note: Start with me da, then say what you want, and add por favor. It is the polite way to order from a stranger.

cards.headline: When you need a small extra

rows.en: Could I have a little bag?

cards.note: ¿Me regala…? is a soft way to ask for small things in central Mexico. It doesn't mean the thing is free; you still pay for what has a price.

cards.headline: When you order tacos

rows.en: How do you want your tacos?

cards.note: Con todo means with onion and cilantro. Sin goes in the same spot, straight before the food: sin cebolla.

cards.headline: With or without

rows.text: Un café sin azúcar, por favor.

cards.note: Con means with and sin means without. Both go straight before the food: con leche, sin azúcar.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Catedral Metropolitana stands on the soft lakebed of Lake Texcoco. Over the centuries its weight made it sink unevenly, so parts of it lean. In the 1990s engineers removed soil from under the higher parts to even it out.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Mexico City, a quick breakfast is often a guajolota: a tamal tucked inside a bolillo, the crusty white roll. It's cheap, heavy and filling, and usually comes with a cup of warm, thick atole.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Pumas and América are two of Mexico City's best-known football clubs, and their meeting is called the Clásico Capitalino. Families here are often split between the two, and the argument at the table can last longer than the match.

cards.headline: About this chocolate mill
cards.note: At a Oaxaca chocolate mill, cacao is ground fresh with sugar, cinnamon and often almonds, and each customer asks for the mix they like. The paste is pressed into tablets to take home and dissolve in hot water or milk.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every 12 October, the Virgen de Zapopan, called la Generala, is carried in a huge procession to her basilica. Families wait on the streets, and many go each year to keep a promise.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In 2021 Atlas won the league title after waiting about seventy years. Many fans cried in the streets and in the cantinas. They are proud of being Guadalajara's local underdogs against Chivas.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Guadalajara, a torta ahogada is a roll filled with meat and drowned in salsa. Tradition says it needs birote salado, a roll with a hard crust and dense crumb, which keeps its shape under all that sauce.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Café de olla is coffee brewed with cinnamon and piloncillo, unrefined cane sugar, traditionally in a clay pot. The clay keeps the heat and gives the drink a slightly earthy taste.

cards.headline: About this art centre
cards.note: This was a textile factory where cotton cloth was woven for decades. Its big halls are now studios, galleries and design shops, where a ceramist works under high ceilings, in plenty of light.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Puebla and Oaxaca each take great pride in their moles, and people from both places happily argue theirs is better. Mole poblano is a dark, rich sauce of dried chiles, chocolate, spices and sesame seeds.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Real Talavera from Puebla and nearby Tlaxcala has an official designation of origin and is made by hand. So a cup in a Puebla café may be a small piece of local craftwork.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: A fonda serves the comida corrida, a set lunch from about one to five, when Mexicans eat their main meal. One price covers soup, rice or pasta, a guisado with tortillas, and an agua fresca.

cards.headline: About this mezcalería
cards.note: Mezcal is made from the agave's heart, the piña, cooked slowly in a pit in the ground. That gives it its smoky taste. Most mezcal comes from Oaxaca, and since 1994 only certain states can use the name.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: People say it to someone who is eating, as a friendly wish at the table or in passing.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Yes, ma'am? How can I help?

cards.note: It is a polite reply when someone calls you, or when you didn't catch what they said.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Back in a moment, I won't be long.

cards.note: You say it when you step out for a moment. Ahorita can stretch to a long time, so don't count the minutes.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The comida is the main meal of the day, eaten in mid-afternoon. Afterward, people often stay at the table for a long sobremesa, talking well after the plates are cleared.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people eat standing at a street taco stand. When the taquero asks what you want on your tacos, you can say "con todo", which means with everything.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Día de Muertos is marked with ofrendas, altars decorated with cempasúchil, a bright orange marigold. Pan de muerto, a bread made for the season, belongs to the celebration too.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Sellers call it out to invite you over to their stall, and then ask what you would like.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: What can we get you, dear?

cards.note: Sellers use it warmly with customers.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: It means soon, or very nearly.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.text: Se acabó el pan. Ni modo.

cards.note: Said when nothing can be done about it.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The main meal of the day is eaten between two and four in the afternoon. At that hour the fondas serve a comida corrida.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: When you walk in where someone is eating, you say "buen provecho." It is a polite wish that they enjoy their meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Mezcal is drunk slowly, in little sips. It comes with orange and sal de gusano.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Guelaguetza takes place in July. It features dances from the eight regions of the state.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Tapatío and tapatía name a person from this city. Use -o for a man and -a for a woman.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Lana is an everyday, casual word for money.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A relaxed way to greet someone you know.

cards.headline: A small word

rows.en: I'll do it in a bit.

cards.note: It can mean right now or later on; the tone tells you which.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Comida corrida is a set lunch eaten in the afternoon, usually between 2 and 4 pm.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People say buen provecho to others who are eating.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Shop owners greet customers with a buenos días or buenas tardes as they walk in.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A polite way to say "pardon?" when you didn't catch what someone said.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: You say it to agree to a plan: fine, you've got a deal.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Come in, come in. There's room here.

cards.note: A warm invitation to come in, said to welcome you.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The main meal of the day is the comida corrida, eaten in the afternoon, usually around 2 pm. Afterwards comes the sobremesa: people linger at the table after the meal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In a shop or a fonda, people greet everyone there with buenas tardes before asking for anything. It is the polite way to begin.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: La Alborada is held in September. It brings fireworks to honour San Miguel Arcángel.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Locos parade takes place in June. There are costumes and dancing, and sweets are thrown to the crowd.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Día de Muertos altars are decorated with marigolds, pan de muerto and papel picado.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: I have a lot of work today.

cards.note: A local word for work.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A local word for money.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A promise to come soon, with a maybe in it.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: You can call a stranger patrón or jefa in a friendly way, for example when asking a price.

cards.headline: When you walk into a small shop
cards.note: People greet shop owners with "buenas tardes" when entering a small shop.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Comida, the main meal, is eaten between 2 and 4 pm. Often it is a menú del día at a fonda, followed by a long sobremesa.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Chiles en nogada are a seasonal dish, eaten in August and September. They are made in the colours of the Mexican flag.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Small purchases are made with coins and small bills. Shops often cannot change large ones.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A polite way to ask someone to say it again.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A quick cry of surprise or agreement; the tone tells you which.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: my son / my daughter, said warmly

cards.note: Said warmly to a boy (mijo) or a girl (mija).

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Every October the city holds the Festival Internacional Cervantino.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: For the Day of the Dead, families make altars and visit the cemetery.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People get around through tunnels under the city. They go by bus, by taxi or on foot.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: My neighbor is from the port.

cards.note: Jarocho is for a man, jarocha for a woman. It is what people from the port of Veracruz are called.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: What will you take, my love?

cards.note: A vendor may call anyone this. It is just friendly.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Pardon? I didn't hear you well.

cards.note: A polite way to ask someone to repeat what they said.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Casual slang, best with friends and people your age.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: At the Café de la Parroquia, people tap a glass with a spoon to ask for milk for their coffee.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Fandangos are gatherings with son jarocho music. Anyone there can sing a verse.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In the evening, people dance danzón in the zócalo, the main square.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: It is a custom to say buen provecho to people who are eating, even to strangers.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Tata comes from Purépecha. People use it for a grandfather or a respected elder, and Vasco de Quiroga is called Tata Vasco with affection.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: On Janitzio, the Day of the Dead is marked with an all-night vigil. Families stay awake through the night.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: At fiestas you can see the Danza de los Viejitos, a traditional dance.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Around the lake, each town has its own craft. The tradition goes back to Tata Vasco.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: It is the custom to say buen provecho to people who are eating.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Evenings are cold by the lake, so people wear a jacket.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Local dishes include pescado blanco, sopa tarasca, churipo, corundas and uchepos. Carnitas come from Michoacán, and ate, a fruit paste, from Morelia.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: the call before a rhyming verse

cards.note: At a vaquería, people call it out just before a rhyming verse.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: the last drop in a glass
Only the last drop is left.

cards.note: A local word for the very last bit left in a glass.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Maya words like this one mix into everyday Spanish here.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: People say mi reina to a woman and mi rey to a man.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people here dress in white. Men wear the guayabera, and women wear the hipil or the terno.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Sleeping in a hammock is a custom here, part of how people rest at home.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: People here go out in the evening, once the heat drops.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Tsotsil is one of the languages many families here speak at home.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Use coleto for a man and coleta for a woman.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Chulo describes masculine things, chula feminine ones.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A casual greeting, the kind you'd use with friends.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Ask before you take anyone's photo. And never take photos inside the church at Chamula.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Many people here speak Tsotsil or Tseltal at home, and Spanish in town.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Each December, torch runners run for the Virgin of Guadalupe.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: How long is the wait at the border crossing?

rows.text: Voy al otro lado a trabajar.
rows.en: I'm going to the U.S. to work.

cards.note: People cross al otro lado to work, study or shop, and they check the wait at la línea first.

rows.en: Shall we go now? Let's go!

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Tacos after midnight are a local custom. When the night is already late, people still go out for tacos.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In Plaza Santa Cecilia you can hire musicians by the song. You choose a song, and they play it for you.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Here you can pay in pesos or in dollars. Both are part of everyday life.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Excuse me, can you help me?

cards.note: A polite way to get anyone's attention.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: You say it when something surprises you.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: A friendly way to agree or to wrap up a chat.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.text: Mi tío vive en el norte.
rows.en: My uncle lives in the United States.

cards.note: Two everyday ways to say the United States.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: A callejoneada means walking the alleys behind a tamborazo. A donkey goes along carrying the mezcal.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Mezcal is drunk neat and slowly, a drink to take your time over.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: In September people climb La Bufa for the Virgen del Patrocinio. The Feria Nacional also takes place that month.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Queso de tuna is a sweet made from cactus fruit. Dulces de leche are another local sweet.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Regio is for a man, regia for a woman. It names a person from this city.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Huerco is for a boy, huerca for a girl.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: My uncle is very tight with money.

cards.note: You say it of someone who hates to spend.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: The Clásico Regio is the big match between Rayados and Tigres, the city's two rival football teams. Local people take it very seriously.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Glorias are a sweet made of milk and pecans. They come from Linares, and you will find them among the local foods of this region.

cards.headline: A word from here

rows.en: Shall we go to the beach? OK.

cards.note: A casual way to say yes, heard in everyday talk.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Plebe or plebes can mean kids, guys or friends, depending on who is talking.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Morro is a boy and morra is a girl.

cards.headline: A word from here
cards.note: Literally it means "salty foot". It is a name for a person from here.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Carnival comes in the week before Lent. There are parades on the malecón, the seafront promenade.

cards.headline: Culture
cards.note: Winter is baseball season here. The local team is the Venados.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: The cantina opened in 1895; its carved wooden bar, tall mirrors and ornate ceiling date from then. A bullet hole in the ceiling is said to be Pancho Villa's, though nobody can prove it.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Alameda Central is the oldest public park in the Americas. It was laid out in 1592 and named for its álamos, the poplar trees.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Metropolitana was built from 1573 to the early 1800s, mixing Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles. It stands on soft lake-bed clay and has sunk unevenly.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Parque México was laid out in the 1920s on the site of a racetrack. Avenida Amsterdam still follows the oval of the old track around it.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: In Mexico City a quesadilla doesn't automatically come with cheese; it's "con queso" only if asked. Huitlacoche, a popular filling, is a prized fungus that grows on corn.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is made in a clay pot with cinnamon and piloncillo, unrefined cane sugar. Chiapas and Veracruz are among the states that grow Mexico's coffee.

cards.headline: About this churrería
cards.note: El Moro has been open day and night since 1935. Hot chocolate comes light, called mexicano, or thick, called español, and you choose how many churros.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Palacio Nacional stands on the site of Moctezuma's residence and now houses the president's offices. Each 15 September the president rings the bell from the central balcony to give the Grito.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: The market is named for the start of the Revolution on 20 November 1910. In its smoky aisle, tlayudas are made on the comal, and tasajo and cecina are grilled over charcoal.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Oaxaca is the land of seven moles, and mole negro gets its dark color from chiles chilhuacles and toasted seeds. Fondas serve a fixed midday comida corrida: soup, a main dish and agua fresca.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Jalatlaco is one of Oaxaca's oldest barrios, with a Nahuatl name and cobbled streets of painted houses. At a fiesta, bells and cohetes start in the morning, and a calenda with giant puppets winds through.

cards.headline: About this site
cards.note: Monte Albán is a Zapotec city built on a levelled mountaintop more than two thousand years ago. Its Gran Plaza has temples along its sides, and the whole site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cards.headline: About this garden
cards.note: The garden can only be visited with a guide. It grows on land that belonged to the Santo Domingo monastery. Cochineal, the insect behind Oaxaca's red dye, lives on nopal cacti.

cards.headline: About this street
cards.note: Oaxaca is a city of printmakers. Francisco Toledo founded the Instituto de Artes Gráficas, a printmaking library and workshop in a colonial house on this street.

cards.headline: About this mezcalería
cards.note: Mezcal is sipped slowly from small copitas, with orange slices and sal de gusano, ground agave worm with salt and chile. Espadín is the common agave; tobalá is wild, rarer and pricier.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: The Mercado San Juan de Dios, also called Mercado Libertad, is one of the largest indoor markets in Latin America. Outside, carts sell tejuino, a cold Jalisco drink of fermented corn masa.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: In a traditional cantina, tequila comes in a small caballito, often with sangrita on the side. Sangrita is a Jalisco invention. Botanas arrive at the table to share.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: The Colonia Americana was built in the early 20th century. Its houses copy American and European styles, hence the name. Its main street, Avenida Chapultepec, has a wide tree-lined walkway down the middle.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi comes from Jalisco. A group has violins, trumpets, a guitarrón and a vihuela, and the players wear the charro suit. Groups wait here to be hired for a song, a birthday or a serenade.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The Hospicio Cabañas was once an orphanage. In its dome is Orozco's mural Man of Fire, and visitors often lie on the benches below to look up at it.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: In the evening the Jardín Allende fills for the paseo, with families, couples and mariachis. Taxis wait nearby to carry people up and down the cobbled streets of the Centro.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Parroquia's pink-stone neo-Gothic façade was designed in the late 1800s by Zeferino Gutiérrez, a local self-taught builder. The church faces the Jardín, the town's main square.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: Café de olla is brewed in a clay pot with piloncillo and cinnamon. A concha or a pan de nata goes with it.

cards.headline: About this art centre
cards.note: Fábrica La Aurora was a textile mill until it closed in the 1990s. Now it is an art and design centre of studios and galleries, and visitors can walk in and look around.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: For tacos al pastor, the pork turns on a vertical spit called a trompo, with a pineapple on top. The method comes from the shawarma that Lebanese immigrants brought to Mexico.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Ignacio Allende was born in this house on the Jardín in 1769, and it is now a museum. The town added his name to its own in 1826, becoming San Miguel de Allende.

cards.headline: About this dulcería
cards.note: This street is the "Calle de los Dulces", where people buy sweets as gifts: camote, tortitas de Santa Clara, muéganos and jamoncillo. Tortitas are pumpkin-seed paste, named after the Santa Clara convent.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Templo de Santo Domingo is one of the best-known churches in the Centro Histórico. It is famous for its richly decorated Capilla del Rosario.

cards.headline: About this market stall
cards.note: Here people eat cemitas poblanas standing up at lunchtime. Each one is built to order with quesillo and pápalo.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Chiles en nogada come in late summer, when walnuts and pomegranates are fresh. Their green, white and red match the Mexican flag.

cards.headline: About this taquería
cards.note: Tacos árabes are the favorite late-night street food here, so a taquería like this is busiest at night.

cards.headline: About this cantina
cards.note: This cantina is known for its pasita, a raisin liqueur. It is served in a small glass with a raisin, a bit of cheese and a toothpick.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: The library began in 1646, when Bishop Juan de Palafox gave his books to the seminary on condition that anyone could read them. Locals call it the first public library in the Americas.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: This grand theatre was opened in 1903 by President Porfirio Díaz. Inside, it is all red velvet and gilded Moorish decoration.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Count of Valenciana built this church, with carved altars covered in gold, in the late 1700s, when the mine next door was among the richest silver mines in the world.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Enchiladas mineras are tortillas dipped in guajillo chile sauce, filled with cheese and onion, and covered with fried potatoes and carrots. They are said to have been the miners' food, cheap and filling.

cards.headline: About this café
cards.note: The famous order is the lechero: strong coffee in a glass. Tap it with a spoon and the waiter pours hot milk from high up. Have it with a bomba, a sweet roll.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Built by the Spanish on an island from the 1500s, it was the last place in Mexico held by Spanish troops, until 1825. Later a feared prison, it held Benito Juárez.

cards.headline: About this stall
cards.note: Picadas are the breakfast of the port: thick rounds of corn dough with pinched edges, topped with red or green salsa, cheese and onion. Gordas, small fat tortillas, are served too.

cards.headline: About this cemetery
cards.note: On the night of 1 November, Purépecha families on the island sit up all night here with candles, cempasúchil flowers, bread and the dead person's favourite food, to welcome the souls who come back.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: This library is in the old church of San Agustín. Its end wall has a huge mural of Michoacán's history, from the Purépecha kingdom to the Revolution, painted by Juan O'Gorman in the early 1940s.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This was the capital of the Purépecha kingdom before the Spanish came. Its five yácatas are pyramids with a round part and a rectangular part, unlike any others in Mexico.

cards.headline: About this food stall
cards.note: Cochinita is pork marinated in achiote and sour orange juice, wrapped in banana leaves and cooked slowly in a pib, a pit oven in the ground. Pib is a Maya word.

cards.headline: About this food stall
cards.note: The kibi is the Arab kibbeh of ground meat and wheat, brought by Lebanese settlers in the late nineteenth century. Fried and eaten with pickled red onion and habanero, it became Yucatecan food.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Inside there are no pews and no regular Mass. The floor is covered with pine needles, and families kneel among candles to pray in Tsotsil. Photographs inside are strictly forbidden.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Chiapas grows more coffee than any other Mexican state, mostly on small mountain plots tended by Indigenous families. The cherries are picked by hand when red, from about November to March.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The marimba is the instrument of Chiapas and a symbol of the state: a long wooden keyboard with resonators underneath, played by three or four people at once.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Plaza Santa Cecilia is named for the patron saint of musicians. People come to hire a group by the song or by the hour, for a birthday, a serenade or a funeral.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Zacatecas is built of cantera rosa, a soft pink stone that hardens in the air. Silver found here in 1546 paid for the cathedral's front, carved like lace.

cards.headline: About this fonda
cards.note: Gorditas are thick corn tortillas, split and filled with stew. The favorite filling is asado de boda: pork in dark red chile sauce, the dish served at weddings here.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This museum holds thousands of Mexican masks, one of the largest collections in the world: devils, jaguars, Moors and Christians, carved for village dances. The painter Rafael Coronel collected them.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: On 23 June 1914 Pancho Villa's army took this hill and the city in one of the bloodiest battles of the Revolution. Three bronze horsemen outside show Villa, Ángeles and Natera.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Macroplaza is one of the largest plazas in the world. Whole blocks of the old centre were knocked down in the early 1980s to build it.

cards.headline: About this riverwalk
cards.note: Named for the springs where Monterrey was founded in 1596, this canal walk runs about two and a half kilometres from the Macroplaza to Parque Fundidora.

cards.headline: About this restaurant
cards.note: Cabrito is the dish of Nuevo León: a milk-fed kid goat, opened flat on an iron stake and roasted for hours beside mesquite embers, never over the flame. Served with flour tortillas.

cards.headline: About this taco stand
cards.note: Tacos mañaneros are small breakfast tacos in flour tortillas, filled with stews like machacado con huevo. Machacado is sun-dried, pounded beef scrambled with egg; drying was how the north kept meat in the heat.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The Virgen del Roble is the patron of Monterrey. Legend says her small image was found in an oak tree's hollow and kept returning there, so a chapel was built on the spot.

cards.headline: About this theatre
cards.note: The Teatro Ángela Peralta opened in 1874. It became a cinema, then a ruin after a hurricane, until the city restored it in 1992. Now it hosts opera, ballet and an autumn cultural festival.

cards.headline: About this street
cards.note: Olas Altas is the oldest beach in Mazatlán, and the malecón begins here. This seafront promenade runs along the sea for about twenty kilometres.

cards.headline: About this lighthouse
cards.note: El Faro stands on the Cerro del Crestón, a hill that was once an island. About a hundred and fifty metres above the sea, it is one of the highest lighthouses in the world.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The park's oval shape follows the track of an old racetrack, the Hipódromo, that once stood here. Today it is a shaded green space with fountains, an open-air theater and many dog walkers.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Work on this cathedral began in 1573 and went on for about 250 years. That is why it mixes styles, from Renaissance and Baroque to Neoclassical. It is among the largest cathedrals in the Americas.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This park was laid out in 1592, making it one of the oldest public parks in the Americas. Its name comes from álamos, the poplar trees planted here.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Diego Rivera began painting the grand stairway murals in 1929 and worked on them for years. They tell the history of Mexico, from the ancient peoples to the twentieth century.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: A fountain with two coyotes stands at the center of this garden. It recalls the Nahuatl meaning usually given for the neighborhood's name: place of coyotes.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This plaza is named for Cassiano Conzatti, an Italian-born botanist who studied Oaxaca's plants. At dusk, birds crowd into its tall trees and fill the air with noise.

cards.headline: About this botanical garden
cards.note: This garden grows on the grounds of the old Santo Domingo monastery and shows plants native to Oaxaca. You see it on a guided tour.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The zócalo is Oaxaca's main square, where people meet and linger. Arcades with cafés line its sides, the cathedral stands on the north, and the government palace on the south.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Monte Albán was a Zapotec capital, founded around 500 BC on a mountaintop above the valleys. It is one of the earliest cities in Mesoamerica and a UNESCO World Heritage site.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Built in the early 1800s as a home for orphans, the sick and the poor, it is now a museum. Its chapel holds murals by José Clemente Orozco, including the Man of Fire.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachi bands in charro suits wait here to be hired, to play a song or a serenade. Mariachi music began in the state of Jalisco, so this is a fitting place to hear it.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: This market is named for Ignacio Ramírez, a writer and reformer born in San Miguel in 1818. People called him El Nigromante. Flowers, produce and food are sold here.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Jardín is the town's main square, right in front of the Parroquia. Trimmed laurel trees shade the benches, and people meet here, sit and stroll day and evening.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The pink stone Gothic towers date from the late 1800s. They were built by Zeferino Gutiérrez, a self-taught local mason. The church behind them is much older, from the 1600s.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This is the house where Ignacio Allende was born in 1769. He became a leader of Mexico's fight for independence. Today the house is a museum of history.

cards.headline: About this lookout
cards.note: El Mirador is a lookout above the town. From here you can see the rooftops and the pink towers of the Parroquia spread out below, a favorite spot at sunset.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Its Rosary Chapel, finished in 1690, is covered in gold leaf and carved stone. It is one of the finest examples of Mexican Baroque, and people come from all over to see it.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The Zócalo is framed by arcades called portales, full of restaurants and cafés, with the cathedral on one side. It has been the center of city life since Puebla's early days.

cards.headline: About this library
cards.note: Bishop Juan de Palafox gave his books to start it in 1646. It is often called the first public library in the Americas, and UNESCO lists it in its Memory of the World register.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This small triangular garden is the town's living room. Trimmed laurel trees shade the benches around a bandstand in the middle, and locals gather here to sit, talk and listen to music.

cards.headline: About this theater
cards.note: The theater opened in 1903 and is named for Benito Juárez. Outside it has Greek-style columns and statues of muses. Inside, the decoration is Moorish in style. It hosts performances of the Cervantino festival.

cards.headline: About this monument
cards.note: This tall statue honors El Pípila, a hero of Independence. By tradition, in 1810 he shielded himself with a stone slab and set fire to the door of the Alhóndiga. He holds a torch high.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The Alhóndiga was built as a grain storehouse. In 1810 it was the site of the first major battle of Mexico's War of Independence. Today it is a museum of local history.

cards.headline: About this university
cards.note: The university grew out of a Jesuit school founded in 1732. It became a university in 1945. Its main building is known for the wide staircase that rises from the street.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This church was paid for by the owner of the nearby Valenciana silver mine, in the 1700s. It is known for its ornate baroque style and its golden altarpieces.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This was the family home of painter Diego Rivera, who was born here in 1886. Today it is a museum with his artworks and with furniture from the family's household.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: The main square has the Palacio Municipal on one side, the Nuestra Señora de la Asunción church on another, and arcades of cafés around the rest. Musicians play here in the evenings.

cards.headline: About this fortress
cards.note: San Juan de Ulúa was built on an island in the harbor to guard the port, and later also served as a prison. Spanish forces held it until 1825, the last Spanish stronghold in Mexico.

cards.headline: About this bastion
cards.note: Once the city was ringed by walls built in the 1600s to defend it against pirate attacks. The Baluarte de Santiago is the only bastion of those walls still standing.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: This museum honors Agustín Lara, the composer and singer behind songs such as "Solamente una vez" and "Granada". His music is among the best known in Mexico.

cards.headline: About this cemetery
cards.note: On the island of Janitzio, families spend the night of November 1 and 2 at the graves of their dead. They keep vigil with candles, marigolds and offerings of food.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Locals also call it the Plaza Grande. It is named for Vasco de Quiroga, the 16th-century bishop who helped each village around the lake develop its own craft. His statue stands at its center.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The basilica holds an image of the Virgin of Health made by Purépecha artisans from a paste of corn cane. Pilgrims have come to see her for centuries.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The yácatas are stepped stone platforms, round and rectangular, built by the Purépecha. They stood in Tzintzuntzan, the capital of their empire before the Spanish arrived, above Lake Pátzcuaro.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This small plaza beside the Santa Lucía church is known for its serenatas: free evenings of Yucatecan music, song and poetry that locals and visitors gather to enjoy.

cards.headline: About this palace
cards.note: The Palacio de Gobierno is the seat of Yucatán's state government. Inside, large murals by Fernando Castro Pacheco tell the story of the Maya and of Yucatán, and visitors can walk in to see them.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Opened in 2012, this museum tells the story of the Maya from ancient times to today. Its building is inspired by the ceiba, the sacred tree of the Maya.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This small hermitage dates from the 1700s. Travelers setting out on the old royal road to Campeche came here to pray for a safe journey.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: There are no pews inside. The floor is covered with pine needles, and families kneel among hundreds of candles. Catholic and Maya traditions mix here, and photography is not allowed.

cards.headline: About this market
cards.note: It stands beside the Santo Domingo church. Maya artisans sell hand-woven textiles here, and the colours and patterns often show which highland village a weaver comes from.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This is the city's main square. Its name, 31 de Marzo, recalls the date the city was founded, in 1528, as Villa Real de Chiapa.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: It stands on a small hill at the end of a pedestrian street. Every December, pilgrims and celebrations around the 12th honor the Virgin of Guadalupe here.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: Once the home of archaeologist Frans Blom and photographer Gertrude Duby, who worked with the Lacandon Maya. Na Bolom means "house of the jaguar" in Tsotsil.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: The cathedral's baroque façade is painted ochre and covered in carved figures. It stands on the north side of the city's main square.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Mariachis gather here in their charro suits, waiting to be hired for a song or a party. Santa Cecilia, the plaza's namesake, is the patron saint of musicians.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: The minaret is the tower left from the Agua Caliente resort, a casino and spa opened in 1928 that drew visitors during Prohibition. Gambling was banned in Mexico in 1935, and the resort closed.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: Built in the 1700s from pink cantera stone, the cathedral has a main façade carved like a stone tapestry, with Christ and the twelve apostles. It is one of Mexico's finest examples of baroque.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: This hill above the city was the key point in the Battle of Zacatecas in 1914. Pancho Villa's forces won there, a turning point in the Mexican Revolution. A monument on the hill remembers it.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The museum stands in the ruins of a former Franciscan convent. It holds thousands of Mexican masks, collected by the painter Rafael Coronel, making it one of the best mask collections in the country.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: This plaza is the heart of a historic center that UNESCO named a World Heritage Site in 1993. The cathedral stands on one side, with the government palace nearby.

cards.headline: About this plaza
cards.note: Macroplaza is one of the largest public squares in the world. It runs for several blocks through downtown, joining the cathedral, government buildings, fountains and the tall Faro del Comercio. It opened in the 1980s.

cards.headline: About this landmark
cards.note: Horno 3 was a blast furnace of the Fundidora steel foundry, which closed in 1986. Since 2007 it has been a museum about steel, set inside the old furnace itself.

cards.headline: About this museum
cards.note: The Obispado was built in the late 1700s as the bishop's residence, on a hill over the city. In 1846 it served as a fort in the Battle of Monterrey. Today it is a regional history museum.

cards.headline: About this piazza
cards.note: The plazuela is named for Juan N. Machado, a local merchant. Old 19th-century buildings ring it, with cafés and restaurants that put tables outside, so in the evening people gather here to eat, talk and listen to music.

cards.headline: About this theater
cards.note: This theater is named for Ángela Peralta, the opera singer known as the Mexican Nightingale. She sang here on tour in 1883 and died of yellow fever soon afterward. The 19th-century hall has since been restored.

cards.headline: About this lighthouse
cards.note: The lighthouse stands on a natural hill high above the sea and is often counted among the highest lighthouses in the world. Visitors reach it by a steep walking trail, and the view over the coast is the reward.

cards.headline: About this church
cards.note: This cathedral was built in the 19th century. Its two tall towers and golden-yellow façade rise above the old center. "Basílica" is a title of honor that the Church gives to special churches.

Good afternoon; use it until it gets dark.
I'll take this one, the one near me.
I'll take that one, the one near you.
How do you want your taco?

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Sale and va are both everyday ways to say OK to a plan.

rows.en: Excuse me, I need to pass.
Excuse me, may I ask you something?

rows.text: No me gusta el picante. ¿Y a ti?
rows.en: I don't like spicy food. And you?

rows.text: ¿Se lleva la falda o el sombrero?
rows.en: Will you take the skirt or the hat?
How much cheese do you want?

rows.text: Medio kilo de queso, por favor.
rows.en: Half a kilo of cheese, please.

rows.text: Un kilo de queso, por favor.

rows.en: Which floor are you going to?
I'm going to the ground floor.
We got here the day before yesterday.
We got here two days ago.

cards.headline: This or that
cards.note: Bien before an adjective works like muy.

cards.headline: Two places: a signature dish

rows.en: Guadalajara: a roll drowned in chile sauce

cards.note: Ahogada means drowned: the sandwich is soaked in sauce. Cabrito is young goat, often roasted over coals.

cards.headline: Two places: a slow-cooked classic

rows.en: Mérida: pork cooked slowly in achiote
Veracruz: red snapper in tomato sauce

cards.note: Cochinita pibil is traditionally cooked underground. The Veracruz sauce has tomato, olives and capers.

cards.headline: Two places: a hearty street meal

rows.en: Oaxaca: a huge crisp toasted tortilla
Puebla: a sandwich on a sesame roll

cards.note: A tlayuda carries beans, cheese and meat on top; a cemita is filled like a sandwich.

cards.headline: Two places: a famous dish

rows.en: Puebla: stuffed chiles in walnut sauce
Tijuana: where the Caesar salad was born

cards.note: Chiles en nogada show green, white and red, with pomegranate seeds on top.

cards.headline: Two places: a tamale

rows.en: Pátzcuaro: a triangular tamale in corn leaf
Oaxaca: a tamale wrapped in banana leaf

cards.note: Both are tamales; the wrapper and the shape tell them apart.

cards.headline: Two places: an agave spirit

rows.en: Guadalajara's state, Jalisco, is tequila country

cards.note: Both are made from agave. Much of the country's mezcal comes from Oaxaca.
